common_name: Sincerity Daylily (1956 President's Cup Yellow-Orange Historic Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Sincerity is a 1953-registered diploid whose frilled, heavily textured blooms hold up well once established.

directions: Sincerity carries deep chrome-yellow, gold-dusted flowers with a faint red flush and a wide chartreuse throat, their crepey petals held open on an extended schedule that lets blooms persist well into evening. It won the President's Cup in 1956 as the most outstanding clump observed on that year's national convention tour, a legacy that predates most of the modern tetraploid daylilies grown today. Plant divisions in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, where the dormant foliage dies back cleanly each winter before rebuilding in spring. Divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep bloom production strong.

common_name: Rare China Daylily (1963 President's Cup Yellow-Rose Blend)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Rare China is a David F. Hall introduction from the late 1950s that still performs reliably in collector gardens.

directions: Rare China opens single, midseason blooms in a soft yellow and rose blend atop tall, dormant-foliage scapes bred by the influential hybridizer David F. Hall. It was named winner of the President's Cup in 1963, recognizing the finest clump observed by attendees touring that year's national convention gardens. The diploid clumps die back fully over winter and rebuild dependably each spring in full sun. Grow in well-drained soil and divide every three to four years to maintain vigorous, free-flowering clumps.

common_name: Sea Gold Daylily (1966 President's Cup Amber-Peach Blend)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Sea Gold is a compact David F. Hall diploid suited to the front of a daylily border.

directions: Sea Gold bears amber-peach blend flowers with a contrasting orange throat on scapes shorter than many of its contemporaries, blooming midseason into late season. Hybridized by David F. Hall, it was honored with the President's Cup in 1966 as the outstanding clump of that year's national convention tour. The dormant foliage dies back completely each winter and resumes growth vigorously in spring. Site in full sun in well-drained soil and divide every few years to keep clumps floriferous.

common_name: Green Valley Daylily (Lenington All-American Fragrant Yellow Self)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Green Valley was bred by Hubert A. Fischer and is valued for dependable performance across a wide range of climates.

directions: Green Valley is a fragrant aureolin-yellow self that opens midseason into late season on dormant-foliage clumps bred by Hubert A. Fischer. It won the President's Cup in 1961 for the finest clump seen on that year's convention tour, and went on to receive the Lenington All-American Award in 1973 for its proven garden performance in diverse climates. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, where the dormant foliage dies back cleanly each winter. Divide every three to four years to sustain strong bloom.

common_name: Lolabelle Daylily (1968 President's Cup Chrome-Yellow Unusual Form)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Lolabelle's semi-evergreen foliage benefits from a protective mulch in the coldest end of its hardiness range.

directions: Lolabelle is a chrome-yellow self with a chartreuse throat, its unusual-form petals twisting on a compact, early-to-midseason scape bred from a Midnight Glamour cross. Blooms are extended and nocturnal, opening late in the day and holding through the following morning longer than typical daylilies. It earned the President's Cup in 1968 as the best clump observed on that year's national convention tour. Grow the semi-evergreen clumps in full sun in well-drained soil, dividing every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Autumn Wood Daylily (1995 President's Cup Peach-Green Polychrome)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Autumn Wood, bred by Hazel Dougherty, carries an unusual peach-and-green polychrome coloring.

directions: Autumn Wood opens peach-and-green polychrome blooms with a matching peach-green throat, held on midseason scapes bred by Hazel Dougherty. Its extended bloom habit lets the unusually tinted flowers stay open well past the morning hours typical of most diploids. The cultivar was awarded the President's Cup in 1995 as the outstanding clump of that year's national convention garden tour. Grow the dormant-foliage clumps in full sun in well-drained soil and divide every three to four years to keep them floriferous.

common_name: Golden Hibiscus Daylily (2003 President's Cup Fragrant Gold Self)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Golden Hibiscus holds its evergreen foliage through mild winters and benefits from winter protection in colder zones.

directions: Golden Hibiscus is a fragrant gold self with an olive-green throat, opening early-to-midseason on compact, evergreen-foliage scapes bred from a Majestic Gold cross. Its large flowers relative to its low scape height give the clumps an unusually full, ground-hugging look in the border. The cultivar received the President's Cup in 2003, recognizing it as the finest clump seen on that year's national convention tour. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil and divide every few years to maintain strong bloom.

common_name: Adorable Tiger Daylily (Don C. Stevens Award Gold with Red Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Adorable Tiger descends from a Love Those Eyes by Tiger Parade cross and carries a well-defined patterned eye.

directions: Adorable Tiger is a fragrant tetraploid with gold petals and a bold red eye above a yellow-green throat, carried on well-branched, midseason scapes with high bud counts. It won the President's Cup in 2006 for the outstanding clump of that national convention tour, and the Don C. Stevens Award in 2008 for its patterned-eye form. Grow the dormant-foliage clumps in full sun in well-drained soil, dividing every three to four years to maintain the heaviest bloom and the clearest eye definition.
sources: daylilies.org Don C. Stevens Award records

common_name: Sombrero Way Daylily (1975 President's Cup Orange-Apricot Blend)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Sombrero Way is a tetraploid bred from a Commandment by Crystal Ball cross with a capacity to rebloom.

directions: Sombrero Way opens orange-apricot blend flowers with a deeper-toned throat on midseason-to-late scapes, and clumps are capable of sending up a second flush of bloom later in the season. Reckamp's cross of Commandment and Crystal Ball earned the President's Cup in 1975 as the finest clump of that year's national convention tour. Grow the dormant-foliage clumps in full sun in well-drained soil, dividing every three to four years to encourage the strongest rebloom.

common_name: Pony Up Daylily (2025 President's Cup Unusual Form Peach Self)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Pony Up is a 2014-registered tetraploid bred by Sandy Holmes and Paul Owen with a distinctive upward-curving petal form.

directions: Pony Up carries very light peach self flowers with a gold throat on tall, heavily budded midseason scapes; its petals sweep upward and outward in an unusual form the hybridizers likened to a pony's raised tail. The semi-evergreen clumps rebloom through the season and were bred in pursuit of an exceptionally tall, pale-colored daylily. The cultivar won the President's Cup in 2025 as the outstanding clump of that year's national convention tour. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil and divide every few years to sustain the heavy bud count.

common_name: Going Overboard Daylily (Achievement Medal Yellow with Green Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Going Overboard, bred by Bill Waldrop, is a vigorously multiplying tetraploid with heavy bud counts.

directions: Going Overboard bears yellow flowers with a green eye and a matching reverse midrib, carried on tall, four-way branched scapes that Bill Waldrop reports hold around thirty buds per scape. The cultivar received the Achievement Medal in 2022 and was later named a President's Cup winner for the finest clump observed on a national convention garden tour. Its dormant, pollen-fertile fans multiply vigorously in the garden. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil and divide every few years to keep the clumps floriferous.
